source_text: Anno quintodecimo principatus Tiberii proponit eum descendisse in ciuitatem Galilaeae Capharnaum, utique de caelo creatoris, in quod de suo ante descenderat. ecquid ergo ordinis fuerat, ut prius de suo caelo in creatoris descendens describeretur? cur enim non et ista reprehendam, quae non implent fidem ordinariae narrationis, deficientis in mendacio semper? plane semel dicta sint per quae iam alibi retractauimus: an descendens per creatorem, et quidem aduersus ipsum, potuerit ab eo admitti et inde tramitti in terram aeque ipsius. nunc autem et reliquum ordinem descensionis expostulo, tenens (descendisse) illum. uiderit enim, sicubi \'apparuisse* positum est. apparere subitum ex inopinato sapit conspectum, qui semel impegerit oculos in id, quod sine mora apparuit, descendisse autem dum fit uidetur et subicit oculos de facto. etiam ordinem facit atque ita cogit exigere, quali habitu, quali suggestu, quonam impetu uel temperamento, etiam quo in tempore diei noctisue descenderit; praeterea, quis uiderit descendentem, quis retulerit, quis adseuerauerit rem, utique nec adseueranti facile credendam. indignum denique, ut Romulus quidem ascensus sui in caelum habuerit Proculum adfirmatorem, Christus uero dei descensus de caelo sui non inuenerit adnuntiatorem, *** quasi non sic et ille ascenderit isdem mendacii scalis, sicut et iste descendit. quid autem illi cum Galilaea. si non erat creatoris, cui ista regio destinabatur ingressuro praedicationem, dicente Esaia: hoc primum bibito, cito facito, regio Zabulon et terra Nepthalim, et ceteri quimaritimam, etIordanis, Galilaea nationum. populus, qui sedetis in tenebris, uidete lumen magnum; qui habitatis terram, sedentes in umbra mortis, lumen ortum est super uos? bene autem, quod et deus Marcionis inluminator uindicatur nationum, quo magis debuerit, uel de caelo etsi descenderet, utique in Pontum potius descendere quam in Galilaeam. ceterum et loco et inluminationis opere secundum praedicationem occurrentibus Christo iam eum prophetatum incipimus agnoscere, ostendentem in primo ingressu uenisse se, non ut legem et prophetas dissolueret, sed ut potius adimpleret. hoc enim Marcion ut additum erasit. sed frustra negabit Christum dixisse quod statim fecit ex parte. prophetiam enim interim de loco adimpleuit: de caelo statim. ad synagogam. ut dici solet: \'ad quod uenimus, hoc age\\ Marcion: aufer etiam illud de euangelio: non sum missus nisi ad oues perditas domus Israhel, et: non est auferre panem filiis et dare eum canibus, ne scilicet Christus Israhelis uideatur. sufficiunt mihi facta pro dictis. detrahe uoces Christi mei: res loquentur. ecce uenit in synagogam: certe ad oues perditas domus Israhelis. ecce doctrinae suae panem prioribus offert Israhelitis: certe, ut filios praefert. ecce aliis eum nondum impertit: certe, ut canes praeterit. quibus autem magis impertisset quam extraneis creatoris, si ipse inprimis non fuisset creatoris? et tamen quomodo in synagogam potuit admitti tam repentinus, tam ignotus, cuius nemo adhuc certus de tribu, de populo, de domo, de censu denique Augusti, quem testem fidelissimum dominicae natiuitatis Romana archiua custodiunt? Meminerant certe, nisi circumcisum scirent, non admittendum in sancta sanctorum. sed etsi passim synagoga adiretur, non tamen ad docendum nisi ab optime cognito et explorato et probato iam pridem in hoc ipsum uel aliunde commendato cum hoc munere. stupebant autem omnes ad doctrinam eius. plane. quoniam, inquit, in potestate erat sermo eius, non quoniam aduersus legem et prophetas docebat. utique enim eloquium diuinum et uim et gratiam praestabat, magis exstruens quam destruens substantiam legis et prophetarum. alioquin non stuperent, sed horrerent, nec mirarentur, sed statim auersarentur destructorem legis et prophetarum, et utique inprimis alterius dei praedi. catorem, quia nec potuisset aduersus legem et prophetas docere et hoc nomine aduersus creatorem non praemissa diuersae atque aemulae diuinitatis professione. cum ergo nihil tale scriptura significet, nisi solam uim et potestatem sermonis admirationi fuisse, facilius ostendit secundum creatorem docuisse illum, quia non negauit, quam aduersus creatorem, quia non significauit. atque ita aut eius erit agnoscendus, secundum quem docuit, aut praeuaricator iudicandus, si secundum eum, aduersus quem uenerat, docuit. exclamat ibidem spiritus daemonis: quid nobis et tibi est, Iesu uenisti perdere nos; scio qui sis, sanctus dei. hic ego non retractabo, an et hoc cognomentum competierit ei, quem nec Christum uocari oporteret, si non creatoris, — alibi iam de nominibus expostulatum est — at nunc discepto, quomodo hoc eum uocari cognouerit daemon, nulla umquam retro emissa praedicatione in illum a deo ignoto et in id temporis muto, cuius nec sanctum eum contestari potuit, ut ignoti (et)iam ipsi suo creatori. quid autem iam tale ediderat nouae diuinitatis. per quod posset alterius dei sanctus intellegi? tantum quod synagogam introgressus et nec sermone operatus (erat) aliquid aduersus creatorem? sicut ergo quem ignorabat nullo modo poterat Iesum et sanctum dei agnoscere, ita quem norat agnouit. nam et prophetam meminerat sanctum dei praedicasse et Iesum nomen domini esse in filio Naue. haec et ab angelo exceperat secundum nostrum euangelium: propterea quod in te nascetur uocabitur sanctum, filius dei, et uocabis nomen eius Iesum. sed et habebat utique sensum aliquem dominicae dispositionis — licet daemon tamen — magis quam alienae et nondum satis cognitae. nam et praemisit: quid nobis et tibi, Iesu? non quasi in extraneum, (sed) ad quem pertinent spiritus creatoris. nec enim dixit: \'quid tibi et nobis\'? sed \'quid nobis et tibi\'? se deplorans et sorti suae exprobrans. quam iam uidens adicit: uenisti perdere nos. adeo iudicis et ultoris et, ut ita dixerim, saeui dei filium agnouerat Iesum, non optimi illius, et perdere et punire nescientis. quorsum hunc locum praemisimus? ut Iesum et a daemone non alium doceamus agnitum et a semetipso non alium confirmatum quam creatoris. \'atquin\', inquis, \'increpuit illum Iesus). plane, ut inuidiosum et in ipsa confessione petulantem, ut male adulantem, quasi haec esset summa gloria Christi, si ad perditionem daemonum uenisset et non potius ad hominum salutem, qui nec discipulos de subactione spirituum, sed de candida salutis gloriari uolebat. aut cur eum increpuit? si quasi mentitum in totum, ergo non fuit Iesus nec dei sanctus omnino; si quasi ex parte mentitum, quod eum legum quidem et sanctum dei, sed creatoris, existimasset, iniustissime increpuit hoc sentientem, quod sciebat sentiendum, et hoc non aestimantem, quod ignorabat aestimandum: alium legum et alterius dei sanctum. quodsi uerisimiliorem statum non habet increpatio nisi quem nos interpretamur, iam ergo et daemon nihil mentitus est, non ob mendacium increpitus; ipse enim erat Iesus, praeter quem alium daemon agnouisse non poterat, et Iesus eum confirmauit, quem agnouerat daemon, dum non ob mendacium increpat daemonem.
pass_a_gloss: In the fifteenth year of Tiberius' reign, He proposes that He descended into the city of Galilee, Capharnaum, certainly from the heaven of the Creator, into which He had previously descended from His own. What order was there, then, that He should first be described as descending from His own heaven into the Creator's? For why should I not also reprehend those things which do not fulfill the faith of the ordinary narrative, which is always deficient in falsehood? Let those things which were once said be now repeated, which we have already retracted elsewhere: whether, descending through the Creator, and indeed against Him, He could have been admitted by Him and sent from there into the earth, equally His own. Now, however, I demand the rest of the order of the descent, holding that He descended. For it is to be seen, indeed, where it is written that He 'appeared'. To appear suddenly, out of the unexpected, has the flavor of a sudden sight, which, once it has struck the eyes on that which appeared without delay, seems to have descended, and subjects the eyes to the fact. And it also makes an order and thus compels one to demand what kind of habit, what kind of suggestion, with what impetus or temperament, and also at what time of day or night He descended; furthermore, who saw Him descending, who reported it, who confirmed the thing, which is not easily to be believed even by one who confirms it. It is finally unworthy that Romulus, indeed, had Proculus as a witness to his ascension into heaven, but Christ did not find an announcer of His descent from heaven, as if He did not ascend in the same ladders of falsehood as He descended. What, then, does Galilee have to do with this? If it was not the Creator's, to whom this region was destined for the entrance of the preaching, saying, as Isaiah says: 'This first, drink quickly, region of Zabulon and land of Nepthalim, and the rest who are by the sea, and the Jordan, Galilee of the nations. A people who sit in darkness, see a great light; who inhabit the land, sitting in the shadow of death, a light has arisen upon you?' But, indeed, it is well that the God of Marcion is also vindicated as the illuminator of the nations, so that He ought to have descended, even from heaven, rather into Pontus than into Galilee. Moreover, both in the place and in the work of illumination, according to the preaching, those who meet Christ we begin to recognize as having been prophesied, showing that He came, not to dissolve the law and the prophets, but rather to fulfill them. For Marcion has erased this as an addition. But in vain will he deny that Christ said what He immediately did in part. For the prophecy was fulfilled in the meantime, concerning the place, immediately, to the synagogue, as it is said: 'to what we have come, let us do this'. Marcion: take away also that from the Gospel: 'I was not sent except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel', and: 'it is not to take the bread of the sons and give it to the dogs', lest Christ seem to be of Israel. The deeds are sufficient for me instead of words. Take away the voices of my Christ: the things will speak. Behold, He comes into the synagogue: certainly to the lost sheep of the house of Israel. Behold, He offers the bread of His doctrine first to the Israelites: certainly, as He prefers the sons. Behold, He does not impart it to others: certainly, as He passes over the dogs. To whom would He have imparted it more than to the strangers of the Creator, if He Himself were not first of the Creator? And yet, how could He have been admitted into the synagogue, so sudden, so unknown, whose no one was yet certain about the tribe, the people, the house, finally the census of Augustus, which the Roman archives keep as a most faithful witness of the Lord's birth? They certainly remembered, unless they knew He was circumcised, He was not to be admitted into the holy of holies. But even if the synagogue was entered in a disorderly manner, nevertheless, one was not admitted to teach unless he was well-known and explored and proven long before, and commended with this duty. They were all amazed at His doctrine. Certainly, because His word was in power, not because He taught against the law and the prophets. For divine eloquence, indeed, presents both the power and the grace, rather building up than destroying the substance of the law and the prophets. Otherwise, they would not have been amazed, but would have been horrified, and would not have marveled, but would have immediately turned away from the destroyer of the law and the prophets, and, certainly, in the first place, from the preacher of another God, because He could not have taught against the law and the prophets, and this name, against the Creator, had not been previously professed as a diverse and rival divinity. Since, therefore, the Scripture does not signify anything of this kind, except that the power and the authority of the word were for admiration, it more easily shows that He taught according to the Creator, because it does not deny it, than against the Creator, because it does not signify it. And thus, either He is to be recognized as belonging to the one according to whom He taught, or He is to be judged as a transgressor, if He taught according to the one against whom He came. The spirit of the demon cries out there: 'What is there between us and you, Jesus? You have come to destroy us; I know who you are, the holy one of God.' Here I will not retract, whether this title also suited Him, whom it was not fitting to call Christ, if He were not of the Creator, — this has already been demanded elsewhere concerning the names — but now, in this dispute, how the demon recognized Him by this title, with no preceding preaching about Him from the unknown God, and at that time, when He could not have been attested as holy by the unknown God, as unknown even to His own Creator. What, then, had He already brought forth of the new divinity, by which He could have been understood as the holy one of another God? Only that, having entered the synagogue, and not having worked anything in word against the Creator? Just as, therefore, the one whom He did not know could not have recognized Jesus as the holy one of God in any way, so the one whom He knew recognized Him. For the demon had also remembered that the holy one of God had been prophesied by the prophet, and that Jesus was the name of the Lord in the son of Nun. He had also received this from the angel, according to our Gospel: 'Therefore, because He will be born in you, He will be called holy, the son of God, and you will call His name Jesus.' But he also had some sense of the Lord's disposition — although he was a demon — rather than of an alien and not yet sufficiently known one. For he had also said beforehand: 'What is there between us and you, Jesus?' not as if to a stranger, but to one to whom the spirits of the Creator pertain. For he did not say: 'what is there between you and us?' but 'what is there between us and you?' lamenting himself and reproaching his own fate. Which, seeing, he adds: 'You have come to destroy us.' So, he recognized Jesus as the son of the judge and the avenger, and, so to speak, of the severe God, not of the good one, who does not know how to destroy and punish. Why have we premised this passage? So that we may teach that Jesus was recognized by the demon, and not by another, and confirmed by Himself, and not by another, as the Creator's. 'But', you say, 'Jesus rebuked him.' Certainly, as one who was envious and petulant in his very confession, as one who was flattering evilly, as if this were the greatest glory of Christ, if He had come to the destruction of the demons, and not rather to the salvation of men, who did not want His disciples to glory in the subjection of spirits, but in the pure glory of salvation. Or why did He rebuke him? If as one who had lied in everything, then Jesus was not the holy one of God at all; if as one who had lied in part, because he had thought Him to be the holy one of God, indeed, but of the Creator, He rebuked him most unjustly, for thinking what He knew was to be thought, and not estimating what He ignored was to be estimated: another holy one of the laws and of another God. But if the rebuke does not have a more probable status than what we interpret, then the demon did not lie at all, nor was he rebuked for falsehood; for Jesus was the one whom the demon could not have recognized as another, and Jesus confirmed the one whom the demon had recognized, while not rebuking the demon for falsehood.

choices.why: The verb 'apparuisse' is in the perfect infinitive form, indicating a completed action of appearing.
The verb 'subicit' is in the present tense, indicating an ongoing action of subjecting.
The verb 'uidetur' is in the present tense, indicating an ongoing action of seeming.
The verb 'exigere' is in the present tense, indicating an ongoing action of demanding.
The noun 'ordinem' refers to a sequence or arrangement of events.

bible_refs.note: The passage quotes Isaiah 9:1-2, which mentions the region of Zabulon and the land of Nepthalim.

pass_b_english: In the fifteenth year of Tiberius' reign, the text claims Jesus descended into Capernaum, a city of Galilee, specifically from the Creator's heaven — the very heaven he had supposedly entered earlier from his own. What kind of sequence is that, to describe him descending from his own heaven into the Creator's first? Why shouldn't I also challenge these details that fail to match the basic credibility of a straightforward narrative, a narrative that is always defective in its falsehood? Let what was said once be said again, the points we have already refuted elsewhere: could he, descending through the Creator and against him, have been admitted by the Creator and then passed from there onto the earth, equally the Creator's? Now I demand the rest of the descent's sequence, granting that he descended. We must check where it is written that he 'appeared'. To appear suddenly, out of nowhere, suggests a sudden sight — something that strikes the eyes at once — which then makes it seem as if he descended, forcing the eyes to accept the fact. That creates a sequence, too, and forces the question: in what guise, with what sudden impulse or measured pace, at what hour of day or night did he descend? And who saw him descend, who reported it, who vouched for it — a thing not easily believed even from the one vouching for it? Finally, it is unworthy that Romulus had Proculus to witness his ascent into heaven, but Christ found no announcer for his descent from heaven — as if he did not climb the same ladder of falsehood he descended on. What does Galilee have to do with him? If it was not the Creator's territory — the region destined for the entrance of the preaching, as Isaiah says: 'Land of Zebulun and land of Naphtali, the way of the sea, beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the nations — the people walking in darkness have seen a great light; on those living in the land of deep darkness a light has dawned' (Isaiah 9:1-2) — then it was well that Marcion's god is also vindicated as the illuminator of the nations, so that he ought to have descended, even from heaven, rather into Pontus than into Galilee. Yet both in the place and in the work of illumination, matching the prophecy, we begin to recognize in the Christ who appears the one who was prophesied, showing he came not to abolish the law and the prophets but to fulfill them — the very thing Marcion erased as an addition. But he will deny in vain that Christ said what he immediately did in part; the prophecy concerning the place was fulfilled at once, in the synagogue, as the saying goes: 'To what we have come, let us do this.' Marcion: cut that from the Gospel too — 'I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel,' and 'It is not right to take the children's bread and throw it to the dogs' — lest Christ appear to belong to Israel. Deeds are enough for me in place of words. Strip away the voices of my Christ: the facts will speak. See, he enters the synagogue: precisely to the lost sheep of the house of Israel. See, he offers the bread of his teaching first to the Israelites: precisely as one who favors the children. See, he does not yet impart it to others: precisely as one who passes by the dogs. To whom would he have imparted it more than to the strangers of the Creator, if he himself were not first of the Creator? And yet, how could he have been admitted to the synagogue, so sudden, so unknown, about whose tribe, people, house, finally the census of Augustus — which the Roman archives keep as the most faithful witness of the Lord's birth — no one was yet certain? They surely remembered that unless they knew he was circumcised, he was not to be admitted into the holy of holies. Even if the synagogue was entered freely, still no one was allowed to teach unless well known, investigated, and proven long before, and commended for this very duty. All were amazed at his teaching. Of course — because his word carried authority, not because he taught against the law and the prophets. For divine eloquence brings both power and grace, building up rather than tearing down the substance of the law and the prophets. Otherwise they would not have been amazed but horrified, would not have marveled but immediately turned away from the destroyer of the law and the prophets, and first of all from the preacher of another god — because he could not have taught against the law and the prophets in the Creator's name without first professing a different and rival divinity. Since Scripture signifies nothing of the sort, but only that the power and authority of his word were the cause for amazement, it shows more easily that he taught according to the Creator, because it does not deny it, than against the Creator, because it does not indicate it. Thus either he is to be acknowledged as belonging to the one according to whom he taught, or judged a fraud if he taught according to the one against whom he came. The demon's spirit cries out there: 'What have you to do with us, Jesus? Have you come to destroy us? I know who you are, the Holy One of God.' Here I will not revisit whether that title also fit him, whom it was not fitting to call Christ if he were not of the Creator — that has been demanded elsewhere concerning the names — but now I dispute how the demon recognized him by this title, with no prior preaching about him from the unknown god, at a time when he could not have been attested as holy by the unknown god, unknown even to his own Creator. What had he already produced of the new divinity by which he could have been understood as the Holy One of another god? Only that he entered the synagogue and worked nothing in word against the Creator? Just as, therefore, the one he did not know could not have recognized Jesus as the Holy One of God in any way, so the one he knew recognized him. For the demon also remembered that the Holy One of God had been prophesied by the prophet, and that Jesus was the name of the Lord in the son of Nun. He had also received this from the angel, according to our Gospel: 'Therefore the holy one to be born will be called the Son of God, and you shall call his name Jesus.' But he also had some sense of the Lord's disposition — though a demon — rather than of an alien and not yet sufficiently known one. For he had also prefaced: 'What have you to do with us, Jesus?' not as to a stranger, but to one to whom the spirits of the Creator belong. For he did not say 'What have you to do with us?' but 'What have we to do with you?' — lamenting himself and reproaching his own fate. Seeing which, he adds: 'You have come to destroy us.' So he recognized Jesus as the son of the judge and avenger, and, so to speak, of the severe God, not of the good one who does not know how to destroy and punish. Why have we premised this passage? So that we may teach that Jesus was recognized by the demon as no other, and confirmed by himself as no other, than the Creator's. 'But,' you say, 'Jesus rebuked him.' Certainly — as one envious and insolent in his very confession, flattering maliciously, as if this were Christ's supreme glory, if he had come for the destruction of demons rather than for the salvation of men, who did not want his disciples to glory in the subjection of spirits but in the pure glory of salvation. Or why did he rebuke him? If as one who had lied completely, then Jesus was not the Holy One of God at all; if as one who had lied in part, because he thought him the Holy One of God indeed but of the Creator, he rebuked him most unjustly for thinking what he knew must be thought, and not estimating what he ignored must be estimated: another holy one of the laws and of another god. But if the rebuke has no more probable basis than what we interpret, then the demon did not lie at all, nor was he rebuked for falsehood; for Jesus was the one whom the demon could not have recognized as another, and Jesus confirmed the one whom the demon had recognized, while not rebuking the demon for falsehood.
